title: Prompts as small, testable specifications
outcome: Write a clear task, trusted rules, examples, and an explicit unknown outcome.
cue: Write the contract first; use the prompt to propose within it.
version: Provider-neutral principles · Ruby 3.3 / Rails 7.2 lab · legacy Ruby 2.7 adaptation notes
useCase: Write a clear task, trusted rules, examples, and an explicit unknown outcome.
benefits: A clear decision and a way to check it.
drawbacks: A prompt-only “never access other tenants” rule fails if the supplied data already contains other tenants. More instructions can also conflict or consume useful context.

trace.title: Task contract
trace.detail:
A prompt is an input contract for a probabilistic component. State the task, allowed evidence, output shape, ambiguity behavior, and limits. Prefer concrete examples over a long list of vague demands such as “be accurate.” Version the prompt alongside the code that validates its output.

Keep trusted application instructions separate from user text, documents, and tool results. Role or delimiter structure helps communicate that boundary; it is not a complete security sandbox. A malicious instruction inside a retrieved page remains outside data even if it sounds authoritative.

Few-shot examples demonstrate valid behavior. Include a normal case, an ambiguous case, and an unknown case. Avoid examples that silently grant access or teach unsupported default values. Test changes on cases that were not used to write the examples.

trace.title: Follow one input
trace.detail: Write the expected typed result before the prompt. Add two examples and one counterexample. Run fixtures, inspect the failure category, and revise only the part that addresses it. Keep prompt version and validator version aligned.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: A prompt-only “never access other tenants” rule fails if the supplied data already contains other tenants. More instructions can also conflict or consume useful context.

recallPrompt: Without notes: Write a clear task, trusted rules, examples, and an explicit unknown outcome. Give a concrete example, one failure, and the check that catches it.
